newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Ostrich farming takes flight in Europe.
newsitem.headline: Ostrich farming takes flight in Europe.

text.p: The ostrich is raising its profile in Europe as beef farmers wake up to the demands of a health conscious public and see the gawkby bird as a potential solution to "mad cow" depression.

A conference organised by the European Ostrich Association (EOA) in the Netherlands last week attracted around 300 farmers from 25 countries. Many were from South Africa, the traditional home of ostrich rearing, but Europeans were there in numbers, interested in an industry that promises lucrative returns.
"If it's done properly you can always make money with ostriches and a lot of farmers in Europe are starting to look at alternatives," said Fred van der Horst, EOA deputy chairman.

Ostrich meat is red but contains less fat and cholesterol than beef. Earlier this year, British Airways acknowledged its health benefits, adding the meat to its first-class menus on transatlantic flights.

"It's healthy and easy to prepare. The market in Europe is definitely growing -- a few years ago you hardly saw it anywhere but it must be on the menu of at least a 100 restaurants in the Netherlands now," Van der Horst said.
He said that five years ago, the Netherlands imported some 100 tonnes of ostrich meat a year. That market has now grown to 400 tonnes, with 1,800 tonnes imported into the European Union as a whole.
Despite this, prices in the shops remain high. Specialist butchers sell top cuts of ostrich steak for up to $40 a kilo.

The birds were domesticated first by the early Egyptians, Greeks and Romans. Farming began in earnest in Africa in the latter part of the 19th century. After a period in the doldrums between the two world wars, the market has grown rapidly again in the last decade.
South Africa still dominates world exports, taking 85 percent of the global market but Australia, the United States and Europe are catching up fast.

According to Francois Mellet of ostrich consultants Animal Technologies in South Africa more than 200,000 birds will be slaughtered there in 1996, and 40,000 killed elsewhere, nearly twice the number in 1995.
But meat is not the prime money earner.
Around 70 percent of the value of a South African bird comes from the high-quality skins that are sold to make luxury leather goods, mostly in the Far East and United States.
The soft, supple hides, which have a distinctive quill pattern, are on a par with crocodile and snake skin and fetch similarly high prices.
The tanned skin from just one bird is worth nearly $300 and is used in most of the usual leather articles such as jackets, footware, wallets and briefcases.
But with an ostrich-skin briefcase retailing at more than $500, these exclusive markets are becoming saturated and the industry is looking to the meat as one potential growth area.
In Europe, rearing techniques have not yet developed sufficiently to produce top quality skins, leaving farmers no option but to focus on rearing for breeding and meat alone.
European farmers looking to get a slice of the ostrich pie -- South African leather and meat exports generate more than $100 million a year -- face considerable start-up costs.
The price of a four-week old chick is around $250. It has to be housed and fed properly, and as a flightless running bird capable of speeds up to 70 km (43.50 miles) an hour, it needs space.
Van der Horst reckoned that from starting a small flock from scratch, it could be five years before a profit was shown.
And start-up costs are not the only problem for a potential ostrich farmer. The industry was rocked last year by a British financial scandal involving so-called "ostrich options".

Private investors were tempted by the promise of huge quick returns and bought into rearing operations, some of which then collapsed. The EOA says this is all in the past and insists the industry has cleaned up its act.
"When an industry is just starting out you get these kinds of schemes, but that's all over now," Van der Horst said.

The industry's image received another blow last week when the European Union banned the import of meat and live ostriches from South Africa, after an outbreak of Congo fever at a leading abattoir, killing one of the workers.
Congo fever, a tick-borne virus, leads to massive internal and some external bleeding, similar to the notorious Ebola virus. Around 30 percent of Congo fever cases are fatal.
The industry is anxious to avoid a crisis and is keen to portray the situation as being totally different to that surrounding BSE in cattle.

South African member of parliament Reggie Oliphant, who represents the capital of the country's ostrich industry Oudtshoorn, said equating the Congo fever outbreak with mad cow disease was "completely erroneous" and called the ban "inappropriate and irresponsible".
Ostrich farmers attending the EOA conference said measures had been taken to ensure that South African meat was completely safe, adding they hoped the ban would be lifted within a month.
